Specific donor marrow T-cell depletion has been investi- gated as the sole form of GVHD prophylaxis.42 In a mult- icentre randomised study, marrow T-cell depletion was found to reduce but not abolish the incidence of acute GVHD, accelerate neutrophil recovery and reduce toxicity compared to transplantation with T-cell replete marrow; however, disease-free survival at 3 years did not differ due to higher rates of relapse in some patients, and a higher incidence of serious infection in T-cell depleted marrow recipients.43 The observation of graft-versus-malignancy effects has led to the development of low-dose non-myelo- ablative conditioning regimens (with or without donor lymphocyte infusions) for elderly or more sensitive pa- tients who might have been unable to receive the standard aggressive therapy.1-3,15,44-48 Safety and efficacy of these reduced-intensity regimens has led to wider application;1 however, the lower mortality rate may be offset by a higher relapse rate,1 and poor engraftment.2 The combination of irradiation, chemotherapy, and immu- nosuppression can cause the development of secondary malignancies in long-term survivors of HSCT.1,49-52 Intracoronary injection of haematopoietic stem cells into the heart is under investigation for cardiac disease,53 intramuscular injection has also been investigated in pe- ripheral vascular disease.54 There is also interest in HSCT in some auto-immune disorders.54 1.
